migration.design: identifier_type is a bare VARCHAR(8) with no domain constraint, so 'adding cik to the domain' would otherwise have been a comment. The migration states the domain as a real CHECK constraint including cik. On PostgreSQL it is added NOT VALID: new and updated rows are enforced, existing rows are neither scanned nor rewritten, so the ALTER takes no long lock and cannot fail on legacy data. Validating it is a separate deliberate operator step (ALTER TABLE identifier_index VALIDATE CONSTRAINT ck_identifier_index_type) and is not done here. SQLite (test-only; its schema comes from Base.metadata, which carries the same CheckConstraint) is a deliberate no-op rather than a batch table rebuild.
migration.domainSource: Exactly what the code writes today: the resolver's _GENERIC_ID_TYPES plus the new cik. A test asserts the migration's list equals app.models.IDENTIFIER_TYPES so the two cannot drift.

guardrailDesign.rule: For every issuer node, the securities linked to it must not exceed the EXACT number of tickers SEC lists for that node's CIK. Not a flat cap.
guardrailDesign.whyNotAFlatCap: SEC's own file shows 6,548 CIKs with 1 ticker, 965 with 2, 371 with 3, and a legitimate tail reaching 27. Any cap loose enough to admit 27 would have admitted the 183-security node; any cap tight enough to catch 183 would reject thousands of real issuers.
guardrailDesign.bound: len(union of the ticker-file tickers and the submissions tickers for that CIK). A union of two SEC lists, because refusing a ticker SEC itself publishes would manufacture false violations.

reasonCodes.multi-cik-fanout: linked securities span more than one SEC CIK — the node is at least two issuers wearing one id
reasonCodes.cik-mismatch: the node claims a CIK and holds securities SEC assigns to a different one
reasonCodes.exceeds-sec-ticker-bound: more securities than SEC lists tickers for the CIK — this is the check that catches the 183-node (6.8x the observed global maximum of 27)
reasonCodes.unbounded-fanout: no CIK determinable for the node at all and it still holds more than one security — the shape the whole name-derived graph is in

guardrailDesign.failClosed: The bound is enforced AT THE WRITE in apply mode (a link that would breach it is refused and counted, never written), not only as a post-hoc report. A post-hoc report would have told us about the 183-node only once it existed.
guardrailDesign.scopeHonesty: A crosswalk filtered to a few tickers does not know that SEC omits the rest — that is ignorance, not absence. Under a filtered crosswalk the check will not claim unbounded-fanout and measures the bound against recognised securities only, so it under-reports rather than inventing violations. Run --guardrail-only with --all for the full verdict.
guardrailDesign.provenBy: The clean-graph test and the synthetic-violation test share ONE guardrail assertion helper. test_guardrail_fails_on_synthetic_over_collapsed_node introduces 5 securities on Apple's issuer node (SEC lists 1 AAPL ticker, bound = 1) and asserts that shared assertion RAISES AssertionError. test_guardrail_catches_multi_cik_collapse proves the multi-CIK half. test_apply_refuses_a_link_that_would_breach_the_bound proves the fail-closed write.

bugsFoundByTheseTests: normalize_cik used zfill(10), which cannot SHORTEN: '0000000000320193' survived as a 16-character string and would have become a SECOND identifier_index key for the same issuer — the precise failure the function exists to prevent. Fixed to strip leading zeros before padding, and to reject a CIK with more than 10 significant digits.
The operator CLI printed its report and then HUNG: app.db.engine was never disposed and aiosqlite holds a non-daemon thread per connection. Fixed with a finally-dispose, so every command exits.

OPERATOR DECISION: run scripts/rebuild_issuer_links.py --all against production as a DRY RUN first to get the real disagreement counts over the live 8,334 edges / 1,323 issuer nodes / 35,918 security nodes. The numbers in this artifact are from a local reproduction of the production SHAPE, not from production itself.

OPERATOR RULING NEEDED on the legacy collapsed edges. Apply is additive by design, so after a production apply a security can carry BOTH a legacy unlabelled name-derived edge and an authoritative cik-exact one. Each is labelled and a consumer can prefer cik-exact, but retiring the legacy ones needs a ruling — and edges are append-only with an ORM guard, so retirement is not a mechanical change this lane could make.
The 1,323 legacy issuer nodes were left untouched. Deduping or merging them (merge_links already exists for exactly this) is separate work.

The per-CIK submissions cache is a deploy-time artifact. Without it the crosswalk's submissions fields are honestly absent, so entity_type / exchanges / sic / ein / stateOfIncorporation / formerNames will be empty in any environment that has no cache (CI included). Populating it on the VM is an ops step, not a code change.
